newsitem.title: USA: Proposed NATO chief schooled in arms, policy.
newsitem.headline: Proposed NATO chief schooled in arms, policy.

text.p: U.S. Army Gen. Wesley Clark, chosen by President Bill Clinton to become NATO's new military commander, is well schooled in arms and diplomacy at a time of tension and change for the Atlantic alliance.

Clark speaks Russian and holds an advanced degree in politics, philosophy and economics from Oxford University. He is also a graduate of the U.S. Military Academy and, at 52, young to be wearing the four stars of a full general.

A former senior member of the U.S. team that helped broker the 1995 Dayton peace accords on Bosnia, Clark is a natural choice to command NATO's military as the alliance deals with a balky Russia and reshapes itself after the Cold War.

"He's the man for the job," said a senior Pentagon official privately. "Clark is bright, scholarly and affable. And he can negotiate with presidents and governments as well as dealing with military counterparts."

The Chicago native, now based in Panama as commander of U.S. forces in Latin America, is expected to receive formal approval from the U.S. Senate and NATO allies to replace retiring U.S. Army Gen. George Joulwan this summer as Supreme Allied Commander of NATO forces in Europe (SACEUR) based in Mons, Belgium.
Despite growing opposition from some quarters in Europe, the SACEUR's job has been held by an American since Gen. Dwight Eisenhower first commanded NATO forces on the heels of the Second World War.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters on Monday that the the United States was already consulting on Clark with the allies. His nomination will require approval of the North Atlantic Council, the political arm of NATO.

"Clark is not a mud-on-the boots kind of guy like Joulwan," said one U.S. Army officer, who also asked not to be identified. "He is very scholarly. He's not a back-slapper, but he's well liked by the troops."
Like Clinton, he grew up in Arkansas and attended Britain's Oxford University as a Rhodes Scholar. But the two did not know each other in Arkansas and their time at Oxford did not overlap.
The Washionton Post reported that Clinton said at the 1995 funeral of three U.S. officials killed accidentally in Bosnia that he knew Clark and that "he hasn't needed any help from me."
Defence officials said Defence Secretary William Cohen, who recommended Clark to Clinton, was greatly impressed with the general, who was among 13 candidates interviewed by Cohen.

Clark would take command at NATO during a tense time for the alliance as the United States and Western nations welcome new members from Eastern Europe and deal with bitter Russian opposition to that move.
Already the United States and France are at sharp odds over a French demand that Washington surrender traditional U.S. command of southern NATO forces based in Naples to a European officer.
Washington has refused to do so, saying that the preponderance of allied force in the region belongs to the United States, including the U.S. Navy's Sixth Fleet in the Mediterranean.

Clark, who will also command some 100,000 American troops in Europe and oversee U.S. military operations in Europe and much of Africa, previously headed the Army's National Training Centre at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas. He has also served as director of strategy on the Pentagon's military Joint Staff.
The general and his wife, Gertrude, have one son.
